articles.headline_raw:
Rupee has fallen and
that is notabad thing
articles.body_raw:
NTHE past year, the rupee has fallen 5.6 percent, from 84.7
to 89.7, against the US dollar. It has fallen even more against
the euro (94 percent) and the British pound (14.3 per cent),
besides also weakening against the Japanese yen and the
Chinese yuan over this period. Thus, the rupee hasdepreciated
against all major currencies in nominal terms. And given the
current low consumer price inflation in India — beloweven that
inthe US, UK, Eurozone or Japan — there has beena declinein
the rupee’s real effective exchange rate (REER) too. The Reserve
Bank of India’s (RBI) datashows the REER index dipping from
an all-time high of 108.1 in November 2024 to 97.5 in October
2025. In other words, the rupee has moved from beinga highly
overvalued to an undervalued currency today.
That’s not abad thing froma foreign tradestandpoint India’s
merchandise trade deficit touched a record $41.7 billion in Oc-
tober. In a scenario oftwin shocks — from US President Donald
Trump’s unilateral tariff actions and the Chinese response in
the form of an aggressive redirection ofits exports tothe restof
the world — an artificially strong rupee isthe last thing theecon-
omy needs. Ifanything, aslightly undervalued currency, which
India now has, would help boost exports and also mitigate the
threat from a flood of cheap Chinese imports. Exchange rates
are an effective shock absorber anda better tool to correct trade
imbalances and improve competitiveness than tariffs and sub-
sidies. Indian policymakers have in the recent past relied ona
combination of overvalued exchange rateand retrograde trade
measures, from tariffs and export bans toquality control orders,
tocontrol inflation and protect domestic industry.
That approach, mercifully, haschanged. The RBI, under the
current governor, has adopted a more flexible exchange rate
policy, letting the rupee float in a calibrated manner. The will-
ingnessto allow steady depreciation has been partly on account
of easing inflation: The fear of a weaker rupee raising the cost
ofimports and pushingup domestic prices has receded dueto
general global defiationary pressures. But a bigger driver, pro-
bably, has been the Trump tariffs and the prospect of a China
Shock 2.0 from that country exporting its excess industrial ca-
pacity. India has acurrent account deficit problem arising from
agrowing mismatch between exports and importsthatcannot
be left unaddressed for too long. The exchange rate policy has
to adjust to this reality.

ticulated and the reality unfolding before
us has grown wider.

Besides institutional imbalance lies
another grave threat: The weakening of
India’s federal structure. Ambedkar and
the framers were unequivocal that India
would be a “Union of States,” a federal
system in which the Union and the states
derived their authority from the Constitu-
tion and not from each other. Today,
federalism itself is under visible strain.
The increasing centralisation of fiscal
powers, reflected in shrinking tax devol-
ution, growing dependence on centrally
designed schemes, and the functioning
of the GST Council, has constrained
the autonomy of states. The partisan role
of governors, along with the rising use
of central agencies against political
opponents in Opposition-ruled states,
has transformed constitutional instru-
ments into levers of coercion. The sidelin-
ing of institutions like the Inter-State
Council further erodes the cooperative
spirit Ambedkar envisioned.
To reverse this decline, restoring ac-
countability must be the foundational
goal of our political life. The battle must
bewaged on three fronts simultaneously:
Politically, through mobilisation and elec-
toral choices that prioritise democratic in-
tegrity; ideologically, through the reaf-
firmation ofconstitutional values against
sectarian narratives; and legally, through
challenging arbitrary executive action and
defending institutional independence in
courts and public forums.
One concrete step that can reinvigorate
parliamentary democracy isto mandate a
minimum of 100 sitting days for each cal-
endar year. Moresittings would naturally
enable thorough debate, ensure greater
time for scrutiny, give the Opposition a
platform to articulate concerns, and rees-
tablish Parliament as the centre of demo-
cratic decision-making.
The Constitution is not merely adocu-
ment to be celebrated once a year, nor is
Ambedkar merely an icon to be gar-
landed. Both represent a vigilance we
must exercise to prevent power from
being absolute. The strength of ademoc-
racy is not measured by the size of its
mandate but by the rigour of its checks
and balances, the independence of itsin-
stitutions, and the courage of its citizens
to defend their sovereign will.

articles.headline_raw:
Ukraine, between terrible
war and humiliating peace
articles.body_raw:
O COUNTRY deserves the fate of Ukraine. Its ter-
ritory is under siege, its people have endured
prolonged suffering, and its leadership is under
pressure to accept a peace plan that largely fa-
vours Russia. Ukraine stands as a poignant rem-
inder of the perils associated with relying on external support
for conflict and security.
Ukraine is incurring heavy losses at the frontline and can-
not resist the mounting Russian pressure. It is facing man-
power and material shortages against the intensifying Russian
assaults. Russian troops have besieged the city of Pokrovsk,
an industrial hub, where Ukrainian forces had fortified them-
selves. This city is crucial to Ukraine’s military supply chain,
given its extensive rail and road network connectivity. Russia
aims to capture the entire Donbas region, comprising the Lu-
hansk and Donetsk provinces.
Inits latest phase of negotiations, the Donald Trump team,
led by Secretary Marco Rubio and Steve Witkoff, is meeting
with the Ukrainian team, led by Rustem Umerov, in Florida.
The initial Trump peace proposal, known as the 28-point
peace deal, has been revised under European pressure. The
new proposal is likely to offer some security guarantees to
Ukraine. The guarantee will certainly not be NATO member-
ship, but the West can provide a formal commitment to
Ukraine thatthe latter willbe protected from a future Russian
assault. The European countries insist on Ukraine’s right to
protect its sovereignty and keep open the possibility of de-
ploying European troops on Ukrainian territory. However,
Russiais unlikely to agree to the deployment of European de-
fence forces in Ukraine.
Another sticking point is the issue of Donbas. Russia wants
Ukraine to accept dejure the entire region of Donbas as its ter-
ritory. Russiacontrols 90 per centofthe Donbas territory, and
the rest remains with Ukraine. For Ukraine’s President Vol-
odymyr Zelenskyy, the withdrawal of troops and acceptingthe
loss of the whole of Donbas is a dangerous proposition, as it
would amount to the surrender of its territory. His regime,
which has become highly vulnerable after corruption charges,
will face stiff resistance from the opposition parties. Ukraine's
chief negotiator, Andriy Yermak, was replaced due to allega-
tions of corruption. Umerov is Ukraine’s new negotiator in
Florida. The survival of Zelenskyy’s regime depends on con-
tinued European financial and military support.
Thetragedy of Ukraine is that itcannot match the Russian
firepower, and if the war continues, it will lose more territory.
On the other hand, no peace proposal can retrieve the territory
that Ukraine has lost to Russia. Moreover, given the current
state of negotiations, there is no guarantee that Russia will
agree to the new proposal. Therefore, for Ukraine, uncertainty

HE SUPREME Court’s Ramjanmabhoomi-Babri Mas-
jid verdict in 2019 put an end to arguably the most
politically fraught title suit inIndenendent India’s his-
tory. In doing so, the Court did not condone the illegal
